<description>一个和平“爆发”的年代？

<description>《资治通鉴》是北宋大政治家、历史学家司马光领衔修撰的我国第一部编年体通史，全书294卷，上起周威烈王二十三年（前403），下终五代周世宗显德六年（959），记载一千三百六十二年间的历史。这部历史名著意在追寻政治得失、王朝兴衰之迹，探究修身齐家、经世治国之道，有着巨大的历史价值，以及知往鉴今的借鉴价值，值得所有人阅读。
本书以清胡克家刻本为底本，参照中华书局点校本《资治通鉴》厘定文字，为全新形式古籍整理四种样式（白话本、新注本、文白对照本、注译本）中最高形式的注译本。是张大可教授历时二十余年对《资治通鉴》全本作新注和新译的成果。其注释吸收了元刊胡三省注本的优秀内容，融合现代研究观点，除传统字音、字义、人物、地理、职官、历史掌故诸项注释外，还结合多种史书，以便全方位了解历史事件与人物。其语译按当时说话人口吻称谓某王、某帝、皇上、皇帝，而在陈述语的译文中，按《资治通鉴》称谓的基础上参照通行的《中国历史纪年表》人物专称增补朝代、国名等作规范语译，如汉朝皇帝用汉高帝、汉惠帝、汉文帝、汉景帝等，增补了“汉”字，余类推。大段陈述语，次用了专称，随后也可用皇上、皇帝指代，使行文简洁而又等同专称。特殊专称，随文加注，如吕太后。此外，译文逐年补上了王公纪年与年号。如此处理，译文畅达、鲜明、历史线索清晰，读者随文认识历史人物而不致淆乱。</description>

Unity 于日前被安全研究员 RyotaK 发现存在严重安全漏洞（CVE-2025-59489）。此漏洞导致攻击者可以通过参数注入实现本地权限提升并执行任意代码。据悉，任何使用 Unity 2017.1及更高版本的 Android、Windows、Linux 和 macOS 操作系统游戏及应用均被波及。

多个大型工作室和独立团队紧急下架或更新产品，包括黑曜石娱乐的《永恒之柱2》和《Pentiment》，Innersloth 的《Among Us》以及 Second Dinner 的《漫威终极逆转》等。微软方面也宣布，将从商店下架一批已不再维护的 Unity 作品，其中包括《Mighty Doom》《上古卷轴：传奇》《Gears POP!》《Halo Recruit》等。 为确保安全，V社也为 Steam 客户端部署了额外的保护。

据彭博社援引知情人士报道，《使命召唤》在2024年的收入比2023年减少约3亿美元，表现远不及微软 Xbox 部门的预期。换言之，加入 XGP 的潜在销售损失大约相当于《使命召唤19》首发10亿美元销售额的三分之一。

对于加入 XGP 的游戏来说，销量下降是相对常见的现象。用户只需支付较低的月费订阅费用就能游玩完整游戏，因此全价购买的玩家自然会有所降低。尽管这种取舍早已被微软纳入财务预估中，但《使命召唤》的实际表似乎促使微软进行收入调整，最终以涨价来推动 Xbox 业务实现更高利润率。

值得一提的是，将《使命召唤》与 XGP 绑定，曾是微软斥资687亿美元收购动视暴雪的核心策略之一。 前美国联邦贸易委员会主席 Lina Khan 指出: 「微软收购动视暴雪后，随之而来的是大幅涨价和裁员，这对玩家和开发者都造成了伤害。正如我们在多个行业中所见，市场集中度上升通常伴随着价格上涨。当一家企业大到不需要在意后果时，消费者的处境往往就会变得更糟。」

YT17 Mon, 06 Oct 2025 15:15:31 +0800 https://www.gcores.com/articles/205245", "RPG+怪猎，果然很有意思：TGS2025《怪物猎人物语3 命运双龙》试玩体验

《怪物猎人物语》系列在《怪物猎人》IP中确实是一个非常特别的存在——它放弃了传统的ACT狩猎模式，转向节奏更舒缓、策略性更强的JRPG类型。在我看来，这其实是CAPCOM意图让《怪物猎人》走出“硬核玩家”圈子，面向更广泛青少年群体所发出的信号。事实上，游戏中的魔物养成玩法以及“猜拳”式战斗机制，确实为《怪物猎人》增添了不少新鲜感和独创性。

当《怪物猎人物语3 命运双龙》正式公布后，我逐渐意识到，《物语》系列似乎已不再满足于仅仅承担“拓圈”功能，而是希望打造一个更偏向RPG爱好者、内容更有深度的全新作品。在上周的TGS2025中，我有幸提前体验了约30分钟的试玩版本，试玩结束后还采访了本作的制作人。

采访文章请参考：《向“更RPG化”再一次迈进：机核《怪物猎人物语 3》制作人采访》

我这次在TGS体验的是游戏初期的两场战斗和一小段地图探索，试玩版本为PS5版，语言是简体中文。

要说试玩版最直观、也最让我印象深刻的地方，无疑是画面上的进步：相比前两作，本作在建模和光影效果的表现上都更具细节。服装的花纹、怪物身上的肌理、甚至地表的碎石……在细节大幅丰富的同时，游戏仍能保持60帧稳定运行。老玩家见到这样的表现，想必会感到“眼前一亮”。

尽管本作依旧采用了高对比度的色彩风格，但在人物建模更接近真实比例之后，《物语3》呈现出的视觉感受，似乎不再像以前那样偏向“儿童绘本”风格。从某种意义上说，这也释放出一个信号：《物语》系列原本承担“扩大《怪物猎人》受众年龄层”的使命，正在转变为“打造一款真正有深度的JRPG”的新目标。

试玩内容位于游戏初期，此时主人公一行正要正式开展骑兵队活动。既然是首次活动，自然少不了系统教学环节。骑乘怪物在地图中移动和采集这次新增了不少功能：例如面对山壁时，可以无缝切换为飞雷龙进行攀爬；又或者在遇到矿物或树木等采集点时，可以使用“撞击”或“喷射火球”来收集素材。

此外，“撞击”和“喷火球”也可以直接触发战斗。而面对蓝速龙这类弱小怪物时，则能通过“咆哮”技能将其吓退，避免不必要的战斗。

从地图规模来看，《物语3》的区域显然更加广阔。试玩流程中也会引导玩家登上高处进行眺望，标记感兴趣的地点。更重要的是，由于本作实现了骑乘怪物的无缝切换，边移动边采集的体验比前作流畅许多。

在本作故事中，主人公一行为了调查“怪物蛋”而踏上旅程，不过试玩版尚未展示随行怪物的养成系统。过场动画中出现了另一个关键设定——“蛋石”。围绕这两大要素，游戏安排了两场难度不高的战斗。玩过前作的玩家都知道，《物语》系列的战斗基于三种攻击属性互相克制的“猜拳”机制，本作同样延续了这一设计，并进行了改进与扩充。

在《物语3》中，角色发动技能不再消耗“牵绊值”，而是改为独立的“体力值”。这实际上是将原本“牵绊值”的功能拆分出来。前作中使用技能会消耗牵绊值，导致难以施展强力的“牵绊技能”。而本作中，牵绊值的积累变得更加容易，攒满后即可进入骑乘状态。当两名队员均处于骑乘状态时，就能发动演出华丽、威力强大的牵绊技能，并打断敌人攻击。

其中，系列特色的“正面对决”系统依然非常关键。当我方与敌人互相瞄准时便会触发这一机制。只要使用克制对手的招式或普通攻击，就能化解敌人攻击的同时给予更高伤害，并大幅提升牵绊值；平手则互相抵消伤害；落败则会陷入被动。此外，怪物发怒后，克制规律可能发生变化，进一步提升了策略性。

在敌人设计方面，本作的怪物新增了“龙气值”属性，相当于怪物的“架势槽”。虽然普通攻击也能削减龙气值，但效率不高。这时，前作中就存在的“部位破坏”功能就发挥了重要作用——在特定状态下，敌人会暴露出不同部位或“弱点”。玩家可以选择合适的武器攻击相应部位，大幅削减其龙气值，直至将其击倒。

击倒敌人后，玩家可以发动名为“同步连击”的“必杀技”，让我方全体成员发动一轮攻击。

由此可见，《物语3》的每个战斗系统都是紧密相连的：体力槽影响技能释放，技能积累牵绊值，骑乘状态大幅削弱龙气值，敌人倒地后又能发动同步连击或牵绊技能造成巨额伤害。环环相扣，玩起来相当有趣。

战斗系统的强化也意味着战斗强度的提升。原本我以为在击败“浮空龙”后试玩就将结束，但乱入的“缠蛙”带来了新的挑战。与普通怪物不同，这次登场的缠蛙是以“厄石化”形态出现的。

在本作故事中，一片原本宁静的大陆正被名为“厄石化”的现象不断侵蚀。被侵蚀的怪物不仅会变得狂暴，还会获得新的力量——战斗中，这些怪物的部分身体会转化为“石化部位”，攻击这些部位会触发“厄石反射”反击。而从游戏说明来看，不同怪物的厄石反射发动时机各不相同，是需要格外注意的技能。

task_details.agent_final_response:
Based on my comprehensive search and analysis of the latest MCP (Model Context Protocol) papers on arXiv, I've identified several highly influential papers and emerging trends in this rapidly evolving field. Here's my detailed analysis:

## **Most Influential MCP Papers**

### 1. **"A Measurement Study of Model Context Protocol" (2509.25292v1)**
**Why it's influential**: This is the **first large-scale empirical study** of the MCP ecosystem, analyzing 8,401 valid projects across six major marketplaces. The paper provides critical insights into:
- **Market reality**: Over 50% of listed MCP projects are invalid or low-value
- **Security risks**: Structural vulnerabilities including dependency monocultures and uneven maintenance
- **Ecosystem maturity**: Clients are in a transitional phase with fragmented protocols

**Impact**: This paper sets the foundation for evidence-based understanding of MCP's real-world adoption and challenges.

### 2. **"When MCP Servers Attack: Taxonomy, Feasibility, and Mitigation" (2509.24272v1)**
**Why it's influential**: This is the **first systematic security analysis** of MCP servers as threat actors. Key contributions:
- **Comprehensive taxonomy**: 12 attack categories for malicious MCP servers
- **Proof-of-concept demonstrations**: Shows how easy it is to create malicious servers
- **Detection gaps**: Current security scanners are insufficient against MCP threats

**Impact**: Essential reading for understanding the security landscape and developing protective measures.

### 3. **"TOUCAN: Synthesizing 1.5M Tool-Agentic Data from Real-World MCP Environments" (2510.01179v1)**
**Why it's influential**: This represents the **largest publicly available tool-agentic dataset** with 1.5 million trajectories from nearly 500 real-world MCPs. Highlights:
- **Scale and diversity**: Unprecedented dataset size and variety
- **Real-world authenticity**: Uses actual MCP environments for realistic task generation
- **Performance gains**: Models fine-tuned on TOUCAN outperform larger closed-source models

**Impact**: Addresses the critical data scarcity problem in open-source agentic AI development.

### 4. **"MCPMark: A Benchmark for Stress-Testing Realistic and Comprehensive MCP Use" (2509.24002v1)**
**Why it's influential**: This introduces the **most comprehensive MCP benchmark** to date with 127 high-quality, expert-validated tasks. Key features:
- **Realistic complexity**: Involves full CRUD operations, not just read-heavy tasks
- **Stress-testing nature**: Even top models (GPT-5-medium) achieve only 52.56% success rate
- **Multi-turn interactions**: Average 16.2 execution turns and 17.4 tool calls per task

**Impact**: Sets a new standard for evaluating MCP systems and reveals current limitations of state-of-the-art models.

## **Current Trends in MCP Research**

### **1. Security and Risk Mitigation**
- **Focus**: Rapid proliferation of MCP servers has created significant security vulnerabilities
- **Trend**: Moving from theoretical concerns to empirical security analysis and mitigation strategies
- **Key Insight**: Malicious MCP servers are easy to implement, hard to detect, and can cause real damage

### **2. Empirical Ecosystem Analysis**
- **Focus**: Moving beyond hype to data-driven understanding of MCP adoption
- **Trend**: Large-scale measurement studies revealing the true state of the MCP ecosystem
- **Key Insight**: The MCP market shows signs of inflation with many low-quality or abandoned projects

### **3. Benchmarking and Standardization**
- **Focus**: Developing comprehensive evaluation frameworks for MCP systems
- **Trend**: Creating realistic, complex benchmarks that stress-test current capabilities
- **Key Insight**: Current LLMs struggle with complex, multi-turn MCP interactions

### **4. Domain-Specific Applications**
- **Focus**: Adapting MCP for specialized fields like bioinformatics, IoT, and healthcare
- **Trend**: Creating MCP interfaces for existing domain-specific tools and workflows
- **Key Insight**: MCP enables natural language interaction with complex domain tools without programming expertise

### **5. Data Generation and Training**
- **Focus**: Addressing the scarcity of high-quality, permissively licensed tool-agentic data
- **Trend**: Large-scale synthetic data generation from real MCP environments
- **Key Insight**: Synthetic data can effectively train models to outperform larger closed-source alternatives

## **Future Directions and Predictions**

### **Short-term (Next 6-12 months)**
1. **Security frameworks**: Development of standardized security review mechanisms for MCP servers
2. **Improved benchmarks**: More comprehensive evaluation frameworks covering edge cases and failure modes
3. **Domain expansion**: MCP adoption in more specialized fields (scientific computing, finance, etc.)

### **Medium-term (1-2 years)**
1. **Ecosystem maturation**: Consolidation of MCP markets with higher-quality, maintained projects
2. **Performance improvements**: Better model architectures specifically designed for MCP interactions
3. **Standardization**: Emergence of de facto standards for MCP implementation and security

### **Long-term (2+ years)**
1. **Integration with other protocols**: MCP becoming part of larger AI-agent ecosystems
2. **Enterprise adoption**: Widespread use in business applications and workflows
3. **Regulatory frameworks**: Development of industry standards and possibly regulatory oversight

## **Key Takeaways**

1. **MCP is still in early stages**: Despite rapid adoption, the ecosystem shows signs of immaturity with many low-quality projects
2. **Security is the biggest concern**: Malicious MCP servers pose significant risks that current tools cannot adequately address
3. **Performance gaps remain**: Even the best models struggle with complex, realistic MCP tasks
4. **Domain-specific applications show promise**: MCP is proving valuable for specialized fields requiring tool integration
5. **Data scarcity is being addressed**: Large-scale synthetic datasets are helping bridge the gap for open-source development

The MCP field is experiencing rapid growth but faces significant challenges in security, standardization, and performance. The most influential papers are those that provide empirical evidence, comprehensive security analysis, and practical solutions to these challenges.

Title: A Measurement Study of Model Context Protocol

Metadata:
- Authors: Hechuan Guo, Yongle Hao, Yue Zhang, Minghui Xu, Peizhuo Lyu, Jiezhi Chen, Xiuzhen Cheng
- Published: 2025-09-29T14:29:20Z
- Last Updated: 2025-09-29T14:29:20Z
- Categories: Primary: cs.CY, Additional: cs.AI

Abstract:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) has been proposed as a unifying standard for connecting large language models (LLMs) with external tools and resources, promising the same role for AI integration that HTTP and USB played for the Web and peripherals. Yet, despite rapid adoption and hype, its trajectory remains uncertain. Are MCP marketplaces truly growing, or merely inflated by placeholders and abandoned prototypes? Are servers secure and privacy-preserving, or do they expose users to systemic risks? And do clients converge on standardized protocols, or remain fragmented across competing designs? In this paper, we present the first large-scale empirical study of the MCP ecosystem. We design and implement MCPCrawler, a systematic measurement framework that collects and normalizes data from six major markets. Over a 14-day campaign, MCPCrawler aggregated 17,630 raw entries, of which 8,401 valid projects (8,060 servers and 341 clients) were analyzed. Our results reveal that more than half of listed projects are invalid or low-value, that servers face structural risks including dependency monocultures and uneven maintenance, and that clients exhibit a transitional phase in protocol and connection patterns. Together, these findings provide the first evidence-based view of the MCP ecosystem, its risks, and its future trajectory.

Title: When MCP Servers Attack: Taxonomy, Feasibility, and Mitigation

Metadata:
- Authors: Weibo Zhao, Jiahao Liu, Bonan Ruan, Shaofei Li, Zhenkai Liang
- Published: 2025-09-29T04:29:58Z
- Last Updated: 2025-09-29T04:29:58Z
- Categories: Primary: cs.CR, Additional: cs.SE

Abstract:
Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers enable AI applications to connect to external systems in a plug-and-play manner, but their rapid proliferation also introduces severe security risks. Unlike mature software ecosystems with rigorous vetting, MCP servers still lack standardized review mechanisms, giving adversaries opportunities to distribute malicious implementations. Despite this pressing risk, the security implications of MCP servers remain underexplored. To address this gap, we present the first systematic study that treats MCP servers as active threat actors and decomposes them into core components to examine how adversarial developers can implant malicious intent. Specifically, we investigate three research questions: (i) what types of attacks malicious MCP servers can launch, (ii) how vulnerable MCP hosts and Large Language Models (LLMs) are to these attacks, and (iii) how feasible it is to carry out MCP server attacks in practice. Our study proposes a component-based taxonomy comprising twelve attack categories. For each category, we develop Proof-of-Concept (PoC) servers and demonstrate their effectiveness across diverse real-world host-LLM settings. We further show that attackers can generate large numbers of malicious servers at virtually no cost. We then test state-of-the-art scanners on the generated servers and found that existing detection approaches are insufficient. These findings highlight that malicious MCP servers are easy to implement, difficult to detect with current tools, and capable of causing concrete damage to AI agent systems. Addressing this threat requires coordinated efforts among protocol designers, host developers, LLM providers, and end users to build a more secure and resilient MCP ecosystem.

Metadata:

- Categories: Primary: cs.LG, Additional: cs.AI, cs.CL

Abstract:
Large Language Model (LLM) agents are rapidly emerging as powerful systems for automating tasks across domains. Yet progress in the open-source community is constrained by the lack of high quality permissively licensed tool-agentic training data. Existing datasets are often limited in diversity, realism, and complexity, particularly regarding multi-tool and multi-turn interactions. To address this gap, we introduce Toucan, the largest publicly available tool-agentic dataset to date, containing 1.5 million trajectories synthesized from nearly 500 real-world Model Context Protocols (MCPs). Unlike prior work, Toucan leverages authentic MCP environments to generate diverse, realistic, and challenging tasks with trajectories involving real tool execution. Our pipeline first produces a broad spectrum of tool-use queries using five distinct models, applies model-based quality filtering, and then generates agentic trajectories with three teacher models using two agentic frameworks. Rigorous rule-based and model-based validation ensures high-quality outputs. We also introduce three extension mechanisms to further diversify tasks and simulate multi-turn conversations. Models fine-tuned on Toucan outperform larger closed-source counterparts on the BFCL V3 benchmark and push the Pareto frontier forward on MCP-Universe Bench.

Title: MCPMark: A Benchmark for Stress-Testing Realistic and Comprehensive MCP Use

Metadata:
- Authors: Zijian Wu, Xiangyan Liu, Xinyuan Zhang, Lingjun Chen, Fanqing Meng, Lingxiao Du, Yiran Zhao, Fanshi Zhang, Yaoqi Ye, Jiawei Wang, Zirui Wang, Jinjie Ni, Yufan Yang, Arvin Xu, Michael Qizhe Shieh
- Published: 2025-09-28T17:53:27Z
- Last Updated: 2025-09-28T17:53:27Z
- Categories: Primary: cs.CL, Additional: cs.AI

Abstract:
MCP standardizes how LLMs interact with external systems, forming the foundation for general agents. However, existing MCP benchmarks remain narrow in scope: they focus on read-heavy tasks or tasks with limited interaction depth, and fail to capture the complexity and realism of real-world workflows. To address this gap, we propose MCPMark, a benchmark designed to evaluate MCP use in a more realistic and comprehensive manner. It consists of $127$ high-quality tasks collaboratively created by domain experts and AI agents. Each task begins with a curated initial state and includes a programmatic script for automatic verification. These tasks demand richer and more diverse interactions with the environment, involving a broad range of create, read, update, and delete (CRUD) operations. We conduct a comprehensive evaluation of cutting-edge LLMs using a minimal agent framework that operates in a tool-calling loop. Empirical results show that the best-performing model, gpt-5-medium, reaches only $52.56$\% pass@1 and $33.86$\% pass^4, while other widely regarded strong models, including claude-sonnet-4 and o3, fall below $30$\% pass@1 and $15$\% pass^4. On average, LLMs require $16.2$ execution turns and $17.4$ tool calls per task, significantly surpassing those in previous MCP benchmarks and highlighting the stress-testing nature of MCPMark.

Abstract:
Bioinformatics tools are essential for complex computational biology tasks, yet their integration with emerging AI-agent frameworks is hindered by incompatible interfaces, heterogeneous input-output formats, and inconsistent parameter conventions. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) provides a standardized framework for tool-AI communication, but manually converting hundreds of existing and rapidly growing specialized bioinformatics tools into MCP-compliant servers is labor-intensive and unsustainable. Here, we present BioinfoMCP, a unified platform comprising two components: BioinfoMCP Converter, which automatically generates robust MCP servers from tool documentation using large language models, and BioinfoMCP Benchmark, which systematically validates the reliability and versatility of converted tools across diverse computational tasks. We present a platform of 38 MCP-converted bioinformatics tools, extensively validated to show that 94.7% successfully executed complex workflows across three widely used AI-agent platforms. By removing technical barriers to AI automation, BioinfoMCP enables natural-language interaction with sophisticated bioinformatics analyses without requiring extensive programming expertise, offering a scalable path to intelligent, interoperable computational biology.

Title: Model Context Protocol for Vision Systems: Audit, Security, and Protocol Extensions

Metadata:
- Authors: Aditi Tiwari, Akshit Bhalla, Darshan Prasad
- Published: 2025-09-26T18:20:08Z
- Last Updated: 2025-09-26T18:20:08Z
- Categories: Primary: cs.CR

Abstract:
The Model Context Protocol (MCP) defines a schema bound execution model for agent-tool interaction, enabling modular computer vision workflows without retraining. To our knowledge, this is the first protocol level, deployment scale audit of MCP in vision systems, identifying systemic weaknesses in schema semantics, interoperability, and runtime coordination. We analyze 91 publicly registered vision centric MCP servers, annotated along nine dimensions of compositional fidelity, and develop an executable benchmark with validators to detect and categorize protocol violations. The audit reveals high prevalence of schema format divergence, missing runtime schema validation, undeclared coordinate conventions, and reliance on untracked bridging scripts. Validator based testing quantifies these failures, with schema format checks flagging misalignments in 78.0 percent of systems, coordinate convention checks detecting spatial reference errors in 24.6 percent, and memory scope checks issuing an average of 33.8 warnings per 100 executions. Security probes show that dynamic and multi agent workflows exhibit elevated risks of privilege escalation and untyped tool connections. The proposed benchmark and validator suite, implemented in a controlled testbed and to be released on GitHub, establishes a reproducible framework for measuring and improving the reliability and security of compositional vision workflows.

Abstract:
The integration of Large Language Models (LLMs) with Internet-of-Things (IoT) systems faces significant challenges in hardware heterogeneity and control complexity. The Model Context Protocol (MCP) emerges as a critical enabler, providing standardized communication between LLMs and physical devices. We propose IoT-MCP, a novel framework that implements MCP through edge-deployed servers to bridge LLMs and IoT ecosystems. To support rigorous evaluation, we introduce IoT-MCP Bench, the first benchmark containing 114 Basic Tasks (e.g., ``What is the current temperature?'') and 1,140 Complex Tasks (e.g., ``I feel so hot, do you have any ideas?'') for IoT-enabled LLMs. Experimental validation across 22 sensor types and 6 microcontroller units demonstrates IoT-MCP's 100% task success rate to generate tool calls that fully meet expectations and obtain completely accurate results, 205ms average response time, and 74KB peak memory footprint. This work delivers both an open-source integration framework (https://github.com/Duke-CEI-Center/IoT-MCP-Servers) and a standardized evaluation methodology for LLM-IoT systems.

  This study is an adaptive, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled
  trial to evaluate the safety and efficacy of novel therapeutic agents in
  hospitalized adults diagnosed with COVID-19. The study is a multicenter
  trial that will be conducted in up to approximately 100 sites globally.
  The study will compare different investigational therapeutic agents to a
  control arm. There will be interim monitoring to introduce new arms and
  allow early stopping for futility, efficacy, or safety. If one therapy
  proves to be efficacious, then this treatment may become the control arm
  for comparison(s) with new experimental treatment(s). Any such change
  would be accompanied by an updated sample size. Because background
  standards of supportive care may evolve/improve over time as more is
  learned about successful management of COVID-19, comparisons of safety
  and efficacy will be based on data from concurrently randomized
  subjects. An independent Data and Safety Monitoring Board (DSMB) will
  actively monitor interim data to make recommendations about early study
  closure or changes to study arms.

  The initial sample size is projected to be 572 subjects to achieve 400
  subjects with a "recovered" status (per the primary objective). The
  primary analysis will be based on those subjects enrolled in order to
  400 recoveries. An additional analysis of the moderate severity subgroup
  (those with baseline status of "Hospitalized, requiring supplemental
  oxygen" or "Hospitalized, not requiring supplemental oxygen - requiring
  ongoing medical care") is also of public health importance. Hence,
  enrollment will be permitted until the date of April 20, 2020 to ensure
  400 recoveries and provide additional data about this important
  subgroup. With recent enrollment rates, the total sample size may be 600
  to over 800.

  Subjects will be assessed daily while hospitalized. If the subjects are
  discharged from the hospital, they will have a study visit at Days 15,
  22, and 29 as an outpatient. For discharged subjects, it is preferred
  that the Day 15 and 29 visits are in person to obtain safety laboratory
  tests and OP swab and blood (serum only) samples for secondary research
  as well as clinical outcome data. However, infection control or other
  restrictions may limit the ability of the subject to return to the
  clinic. In this case, Day 15 and 29 visits may be conducted by phone,
  and only clinical data will be obtained. The Day 22 visit does not have
  laboratory tests or collection of samples and may also be conducted by
  phone.

  All subjects will undergo a series of efficacy, safety, and laboratory
  assessments. Safety laboratory tests and blood (serum and plasma)
  research samples and oropharyngeal (OP) swabs will be obtained on Days 1
  (prior to infusion) and Days 3, 5, 8, and 11 (while hospitalized). OP
  swabs and blood (serum only) plus safety laboratory tests will be
  collected on Day 15 and 29 (if the subject attends an in-person visit or
  are still hospitalized).

  The primary outcome is time to recovery by Day 29. A key secondary
  outcome evaluates treatment-related improvements in the 8-point ordinal
  scale at Day 15. As little is known about the clinical course of
  COVID-19, a pilot study will be used for a blinded sample size
  reassessment.

# Research Summary: NCT04280705 - Adaptive COVID-19 Treatment Trial (ACTT-1)

## Basic Trial Information

- **NCT ID**: NCT04280705
- **Brief Title**: Adaptive COVID-19 Treatment Trial (ACTT)
- **Official Title**: A Multicenter, Adaptive, Randomized Blinded Controlled Trial of the Safety and Efficacy of Investigational Therapeutics for the Treatment of COVID-19 in Hospitalized Adults
- **Study ID**: 20-0006
- **Sponsor**: National Institute of Allergy and Infectious Diseases (NIAID)
- **Overall Status**: COMPLETED
- **Study Period**: February 21, 2020 - May 21, 2020
- **Phase**: Phase 3
- **Study Type**: Interventional
- **Enrollment**: 1,062 participants

## Study Design

### Methodology
- **Design**: Multicenter, adaptive, randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial
- **Randomization**: 1:1 allocation to remdesivir or placebo
- **Masking**: Double-blind (participants and investigators)
- **Adaptive Features**: 
  - Interim monitoring for early stopping for futility, efficacy, or safety
  - Ability to introduce new arms and modify control arms
  - Sample size reassessment based on pilot data

### Study Population
- **Inclusion Criteria**:
  - Hospitalized adults (≥18 years) with COVID-19 symptoms
  - Laboratory-confirmed SARS-CoV-2 infection (PCR or commercial assay)
  - Illness of any duration with at least one of:
    - Radiographic infiltrates
    - SpO₂ ≤ 94% on room air
    - Requiring supplemental oxygen
    - Requiring mechanical ventilation

- **Exclusion Criteria**:
  - ALT or AST > 5 times upper limit of normal
  - eGFR < 30 ml/min (including dialysis)
  - Pregnancy or breastfeeding
  - Anticipated discharge within 72 hours
  - Allergy to study medication

### Intervention
- **Experimental Arm**: Remdesivir 200 mg IV on Day 1, followed by 100 mg IV daily for up to 10 days
- **Control Arm**: Matching placebo administered identically
- **Treatment Duration**: Up to 10 days while hospitalized

## Primary Outcomes

### Time to Recovery
- **Definition**: First day satisfying one of:
  - Hospitalized, not requiring supplemental oxygen - no longer requiring ongoing medical care
  - Not hospitalized, limitation on activities and/or requiring home oxygen
  - Not hospitalized, no limitations on activities

### Key Results
- **Remdesivir Group**: Median 10 days (95% CI: 9-11)
- **Placebo Group**: Median 15 days (95% CI: 13-18)
- **Hazard Ratio**: 1.29 (95% CI: 1.12-1.49, p < 0.001)

### Subgroup Analyses
- **By Race**: Consistent benefit across racial groups
- **By Ethnicity**: Benefit in both Hispanic/Latino and non-Hispanic/Latino participants
- **By Sex**: Similar benefits in males and females

## Secondary Outcomes

### Clinical Status Improvements
- **Time to improvement by ≥1 category**: Median 7 days (remdesivir) vs 9 days (placebo), p = 0.002
- **Time to improvement by ≥2 categories**: Median 11 days (remdesivir) vs 14 days (placebo), p < 0.001
- **Time to discharge or NEWS ≤2**: Median 8 days (remdesivir) vs 12 days (placebo), p < 0.001

### Mortality
- **14-day mortality**: 7% (remdesivir) vs 12% (placebo)
- **29-day mortality**: 11% (remdesivir) vs 15% (placebo)

### Clinical Outcomes
- **Duration of hospitalization**: Median 12 days (remdesivir) vs 17 days (placebo)
- **Reduced need for new oxygen therapy**: 36% vs 44%
- **Reduced need for new ventilation**: 13% vs 23%

## Participant Demographics

### Baseline Characteristics (n = 1,062)
- **Age**: Mean 58.9 years (SD 15.0)
  - 18-65 years: 678 (63.8%)
  - ≥65 years: 384 (36.2%)
- **Sex**: Male 684 (64.4%), Female 378 (35.6%)
- **Race/Ethnicity**:
  - White: 566 (53.3%)
  - Black/African American: 226 (21.3%)
  - Asian: 135 (12.7%)
  - Hispanic/Latino: 250 (23.5%)
- **Disease Severity**:
  - Mild-to-moderate: 105 (9.9%)
  - Severe: 957 (90.1%)

### Geographic Distribution
- **United States**: 837 participants (78.8%)
- **International Sites**: 225 participants (21.2%) across 10 countries
  - Denmark, Germany, Greece, Japan, Mexico, Singapore, South Korea, Spain, United Kingdom

## Safety and Adverse Events

### Serious Adverse Events (SAEs)
- **Remdesivir Group**: 24% of participants
- **Placebo Group**: 32% of participants (p = 0.010)

### Grade 3-4 Adverse Events
- **Remdesivir Group**: 51% of participants
- **Placebo Group**: 57% of participants (p = 0.058)

### Common Laboratory Abnormalities
- **Decreased glomerular filtration rate**: 55 (remdesivir) vs 74 (placebo)
- **Decreased hemoglobin**: 48 (remdesivir) vs 62 (placebo)
- **Decreased lymphocyte count**: 44 (remdesivir) vs 54 (placebo)
- **Increased aspartate aminotransferase**: 18 (remdesivir) vs 33 (placebo)

### Treatment Discontinuation
- **Remdesivir Group**: 4.4% discontinued early
- **Placebo Group**: 2.5% discontinued early

## Key Findings and Significance

### Efficacy Results
1. **Faster Recovery**: Remdesivir significantly reduced time to recovery by 5 days (31% reduction)
2. **Clinical Improvement**: Accelerated clinical status improvements across multiple measures
3. **Mortality Trend**: Lower mortality rates, though not statistically significant at 29 days
4. **Resource Utilization**: Reduced duration of hospitalization and need for intensive respiratory support

### Safety Profile
- **Generally Well-Tolerated**: No significant increase in serious adverse events
- **Manageable Side Effects**: Laboratory abnormalities were consistent with underlying COVID-19
- **Low Discontinuation Rate**: Most participants completed the full treatment course

### Subgroup Consistency
- Benefits observed across all demographic subgroups
- Consistent effects regardless of disease severity at baseline
- No evidence of differential treatment effects by age, sex, or race/ethnicity

## Study Strengths

### Methodological Rigor
- **Randomized, Double-Blind Design**: Minimized bias in treatment assessment
- **Adaptive Platform**: Efficient evaluation during rapidly evolving pandemic
- **Multicenter International**: Enhanced generalizability of findings
- **Comprehensive Outcome Assessment**: Multiple clinical and laboratory endpoints

### Statistical Power
- **Adequate Sample Size**: 1,062 participants provided robust statistical power
- **Pre-Specified Analyses**: Primary and secondary outcomes clearly defined
- **Adjustment for Multiple Comparisons**: Appropriate statistical methods employed

## Limitations

### Study Constraints
- **Early Pandemic Context**: Conducted before variants of concern emerged
- **Limited Treatment Duration**: 10-day course may not be optimal for all patients
- **Evolving Standard of Care**: Background treatments changed during study period
- **Short Follow-up**: 29-day follow-up may miss long-term outcomes

### Generalizability Considerations
- **Hospitalized Population**: Results may not apply to mild outpatient cases
- **Specific Patient Groups**: Limited data on immunocompromised or pediatric patients
- **Geographic Variation**: Most participants from the United States

## Clinical Impact and Implications

### Practice-Changing Results
- **First Effective Antiviral**: Established remdesivir as the first proven effective treatment for COVID-19
- **Treatment Standard**: Became foundation for COVID-19 treatment guidelines worldwide
- **Platform Validation**: Demonstrated effectiveness of adaptive trial design for pandemic response

### Regulatory Impact
- **FDA Emergency Use Authorization**: Granted May 1, 2020
- **Global Regulatory Approvals**: Approved in multiple countries based on these results
- **Treatment Guidelines**: Incorporated into major clinical practice guidelines

### Scientific Contributions
- **Proof of Concept**: Demonstrated that antiviral therapy could improve COVID-19 outcomes
- **Platform Development**: Established template for rapid therapeutic evaluation
- **Methodological Innovation**: Advanced adaptive trial design for infectious disease research

## Publications and Citations

### Primary Publication
Beigel JH, Tomashek KM, Dodd LE, et al. Remdesivir for the Treatment of Covid-19 - Final Report. *N Engl J Med*. 2020;383(19):1813-1826. doi: 10.1056/NEJMoa2007764

### Key Subsequent Analyses
- Potter GE, et al. Temporal Improvements in COVID-19 Outcomes for Hospitalized Adults. *Ann Intern Med*. 2022;175(12):1716-1727.
- Hedskog C, et al. Viral Resistance Analyses From the Remdesivir Phase 3 Adaptive COVID-19 Treatment Trial-1. *J Infect Dis*. 2023;228(9):1263-1273.
- Singh K, et al. SARS-CoV-2 RNA and Nucleocapsid Antigen Are Blood Biomarkers Associated With Severe Disease Outcomes That Improve in Response to Remdesivir. *J Infect Dis*. 2024;230(3):624-634.

## Conclusion

The ACTT-1 trial (NCT04280705) represents a landmark achievement in COVID-19 therapeutic research. As the first large-scale, randomized controlled trial to demonstrate efficacy of an antiviral treatment for COVID-19, it provided crucial evidence that supported the emergency use authorization and subsequent approval of remdesivir. The trial's adaptive design, rigorous methodology, and comprehensive assessment of clinical outcomes established a new standard for pandemic research and directly influenced clinical practice worldwide. The findings demonstrated that remdesivir significantly accelerated recovery time in hospitalized COVID-19 patients, with a favorable safety profile, making it a cornerstone of COVID-19 treatment during the pandemic.

---

*This research summary was generated from ClinicalTrials.gov data and represents the final results of the ACTT-1 trial, which was completed in May 2020.*

args.content:
# LeetCode Daily Challenge: Swim in Rising Water

**Date:** October 6, 2025  
**Problem ID:** 778  
**Difficulty:** Hard  
**Acceptance Rate:** 65.7%

## Problem Statement

You are given an `n x n` integer matrix `grid` where each value `grid[i][j]` represents the elevation at that point `(i, j)`.

It starts raining, and water gradually rises over time. At time `t`, the water level is `t`, meaning **any** cell with elevation less than equal to `t` is submerged or reachable.

You can swim from a square to another 4-directionally adjacent square if and only if the elevation of both squares individually are at most `t`. You can swim infinite distances in zero time. Of course, you must stay within the boundaries of the grid during your swim.

Return **the minimum time until you can reach the bottom right square** `(n - 1, n - 1)` if you start at the top left square `(0, 0)`.

## Examples

### Example 1
```
Input: grid = [[0,2],[1,3]]
Output: 3
```
**Explanation:**
- At time 0, you are in grid location (0, 0).
- You cannot go anywhere else because 4-directionally adjacent neighbors have a higher elevation than t = 0.
- You cannot reach point (1, 1) until time 3.
- When the depth of water is 3, we can swim anywhere inside the grid.

### Example 2
```
Input: grid = [[0,1,2,3,4],[24,23,22,21,5],[12,13,14,15,16],[11,17,18,19,20],[10,9,8,7,6]]
Output: 16
```
**Explanation:** The final route is shown. We need to wait until time 16 so that (0, 0) and (4, 4) are connected.

## Constraints

- `n == grid.length`
- `n == grid[i].length`
- `1 <= n <= 50`
- `0 <= grid[i][j] < n²`
- Each value `grid[i][j]` is **unique**.

## Key Insights

1. **Binary Search on Time**: The answer must be between 0 and n²-1 (since all values are unique and less than n²). We can binary search on the time and check if a path exists.

2. **Dijkstra's Algorithm**: This is essentially finding the path with the minimum maximum elevation along the path. We can use a priority queue to always expand the path with the smallest maximum elevation so far.

3. **Union Find**: We can process cells in increasing order of elevation and use union-find to check when the start and end become connected.

4. **BFS with Priority Queue**: Similar to Dijkstra's, we can use a min-heap to always visit the cell with the smallest elevation first.

## Solution Approaches

### Approach 1: Binary Search + BFS/DFS

**Intuition:** Since the answer is bounded between 0 and n²-1, we can binary search on the time and check if a path exists from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1) where all cells on the path have elevation ≤ current time.

**Algorithm:**
1. Set `left = 0`, `right = n*n - 1`
2. While `left < right`:
   - `mid = left + (right - left) / 2`
   - Check if there's a path from (0,0) to (n-1,n-1) with all cells ≤ mid
   - If path exists, `right = mid`, else `left = mid + 1`
3. Return `left`

**Time Complexity:** O(n² log(n²)) = O(n² log n)
**Space Complexity:** O(n²)

### Approach 2: Dijkstra's Algorithm (Optimal)

**Intuition:** We want to find the path where the maximum elevation along the path is minimized. This is similar to finding the path with minimum "maximum weight" which Dijkstra's can solve.

**Algorithm:**
1. Use a priority queue (min-heap) storing `(max_elevation, row, col)`
2. Start from (0,0) with max_elevation = grid[0][0]
3. For each neighbor, calculate new_max = max(current_max, neighbor_elevation)
4. If we found a better (smaller) max_elevation for a cell, update and push to heap
5. When we reach (n-1,n-1), return the max_elevation

**Time Complexity:** O(n² log n²) = O(n² log n)
**Space Complexity:** O(n²)

### Approach 3: Union Find

**Intuition:** Process cells in increasing order of elevation and use union-find to connect adjacent cells. The answer is when start and end become connected.

**Algorithm:**
1. Create a list of all cells with their elevations and sort by elevation
2. Initialize union-find structure
3. Process cells in increasing order of elevation:
   - For each cell, connect it to adjacent cells that have been processed
   - After each connection, check if start and end are connected
4. Return the elevation when start and end first become connected

**Time Complexity:** O(n² log n²) = O(n² log n)
**Space Complexity:** O(n²)

## Code Implementations

### Python Implementation (Dijkstra's Algorithm)

```python
import heapq
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def swimInWater(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        
        # Priority queue: (max_elevation, row, col)
        heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
        visited = set()
        visited.add((0, 0))
        
        while heap:
            max_elev, row, col = heapq.heappop(heap)
            
            # If we reached the destination
            if row == n - 1 and col == n - 1:
                return max_elev
            
            # Check all 4 directions
            for dr, dc in directions:
                new_row, new_col = row + dr, col + dc
                
                # Check bounds and if not visited
                if (0 <= new_row < n and 0 <= new_col < n and 
                    (new_row, new_col) not in visited):
                    
                    new_max = max(max_elev, grid[new_row][new_col])
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (new_max, new_row, new_col))
                    visited.add((new_row, new_col))
        
        return -1  # Should not reach here for valid input
```

### Python Implementation (Binary Search + BFS)

```python
from typing import List
from collections import deque

class Solution:
    def swimInWater(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        
        def can_swim(time_limit):
            """Check if we can reach (n-1, n-1) with given time limit"""
            if grid[0][0] > time_limit or grid[n-1][n-1] > time_limit:
                return False
            
            visited = [[False] * n for _ in range(n)]
            queue = deque([(0, 0)])
            visited[0][0] = True
            
            while queue:
                row, col = queue.popleft()
                
                if row == n - 1 and col == n - 1:
                    return True
                
                for dr, dc in directions:
                    new_row, new_col = row + dr, col + dc
                    
                    if (0 <= new_row < n and 0 <= new_col < n and 
                        not visited[new_row][new_col] and 
                        grid[new_row][new_col] <= time_limit):
                        
                        visited[new_row][new_col] = True
                        queue.append((new_row, new_col))
            
            return False
        
        # Binary search for the minimum time
        left, right = 0, n * n - 1
        
        while left < right:
            mid = left + (right - left) // 2
            if can_swim(mid):
                right = mid
            else:
                left = mid + 1
        
        return left
```

### Python Implementation (Union Find)

```python
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def swimInWater(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        
        # Create list of (elevation, row, col) and sort by elevation
        cells = []
        for i in range(n):
            for j in range(n):
                cells.append((grid[i][j], i, j))
        cells.sort()
        
        # Union Find data structure
        parent = list(range(n * n))
        rank = [0] * (n * n)
        
        def find(x):
            if parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = find(parent[x])
            return parent[x]
        
        def union(x, y):
            px, py = find(x), find(y)
            if px == py:
                return False
            if rank[px] < rank[py]:
                parent[px] = py
            elif rank[px] > rank[py]:
                parent[py] = px
            else:
                parent[py] = px
                rank[px] += 1
            return True
        
        # Directions for adjacent cells
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        
        # Process cells in increasing order of elevation
        for elevation, i, j in cells:
            # Current cell index
            current = i * n + j
            
            # Check all adjacent cells
            for di, dj in directions:
                ni, nj = i + di, j + dj
                if 0 <= ni < n and 0 <= nj < n and grid[ni][nj] <= elevation:
                    neighbor = ni * n + nj
                    union(current, neighbor)
            
            # Check if start and end are connected
            if find(0) == find(n * n - 1):
                return elevation
        
        return n * n - 1  # Should not reach here
```

## Complexity Analysis

| Approach | Time Complexity | Space Complexity | Notes |
|----------|-----------------|------------------|-------|
| Binary Search + BFS | O(n² log n²) = O(n² log n) | O(n²) | Simple to understand, good for interviews |
| Dijkstra's Algorithm | O(n² log n²) = O(n² log n) | O(n²) | Most efficient in practice, optimal solution |
| Union Find | O(n² log n²) = O(n² log n) | O(n²) | Elegant approach, good for connectivity problems |

## Edge Cases and Considerations

1. **Single Cell Grid**: When n = 1, the answer is always grid[0][0]
2. **Already Connected Path**: If there's a path where all cells have elevation ≤ max(grid[0][0], grid[n-1][n-1])
3. **Worst Case Path**: When the path must go through the highest elevation cell
4. **Unique Values**: The constraint that all values are unique simplifies some approaches

## Visual Walkthrough

Let's walk through Example 2 step by step:

```
Grid:
[[ 0,  1,  2,  3,  4],
 [24, 23, 22, 21,  5],
 [12, 13, 14, 15, 16],
 [11, 17, 18, 19, 20],
 [10,  9,  8,  7,  6]]
```

**Dijkstra's Algorithm Execution:**

1. Start at (0,0) with max_elevation = 0
2. From (0,0), can go to (0,1) with max_elevation = max(0,1) = 1
3. Continue expanding, always choosing the path with smallest current max_elevation
4. The optimal path will be: (0,0) → (0,1) → (0,2) → (0,3) → (0,4) → (1,4) → (2,4) → (2,3) → (2,2) → (2,1) → (2,0) → (3,0) → (4,0) → (4,1) → (4,2) → (4,3) → (4,4)
5. The maximum elevation along this path is 16

**Why 16?**
- The path must go through cell (2,4) which has elevation 16
- This is the bottleneck - we need to wait until time 16 for this cell to be reachable
- All other cells on the optimal path have elevation ≤ 16

## Optimization Tips

1. **Early Termination**: In Dijkstra's algorithm, we can terminate as soon as we reach the destination
2. **Priority Queue Optimization**: Use a more efficient heap implementation if available
3. **Memory Optimization**: For large grids, consider using iterative DFS instead of BFS to avoid queue memory issues
4. **Bidirectional Search**: For very large grids, consider searching from both start and end simultaneously

## Common Mistakes

1. **Wrong Binary Search Bounds**: Forgetting that the maximum possible answer is n²-1
2. **Incorrect Path Validation**: Not checking both the current cell and destination cell in binary search approach
3. **Priority Queue Usage**: Using max-heap instead of min-heap in Dijkstra's approach
4. **Union Find Implementation**: Forgetting to check adjacent cells that have already been processed
5. **Direction Handling**: Missing some of the 4 directions or going out of bounds

## Related Problems

1. **Path With Minimum Effort** (Medium) - Similar concept but with absolute difference constraint
2. **Cheapest Flights Within K Stops** (Medium) - Uses similar Dijkstra's approach
3. **Network Delay Time** (Medium) - Another Dijkstra's application
4. **Surrounded Regions** (Medium) - Uses BFS/DFS for connectivity
5. **Number of Islands** (Medium) - Basic connectivity problem

## Interview Tips

1. **Start with the simplest approach** (Binary Search + BFS) as it's easier to explain
2. **Mention all three approaches** to show comprehensive understanding
3. **Explain the trade-offs** between different approaches
4. **Draw the grid** and walk through a small example
5. **Discuss edge cases** and how your solution handles them
6. **Consider follow-up questions** like "What if the grid is very large?" or "What if we have multiple sources/destinations?"

## Final Answer

The most efficient and recommended solution is **Dijkstra's Algorithm** as it directly solves the problem of finding the path with the minimum maximum elevation. Here's the optimal implementation:

```python
import heapq
from typing import List

class Solution:
    def swimInWater(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        heap = [(grid[0][0], 0, 0)]
        visited = set([(0, 0)])
        directions = [(0, 1), (1, 0), (0, -1), (-1, 0)]
        
        while heap:
            max_elev, row, col = heapq.heappop(heap)
            
            if row == n - 1 and col == n - 1:
                return max_elev
            
            for dr, dc in directions:
                new_row, new_col = row + dr, col + dc
                if (0 <= new_row < n and 0 <= new_col < n and 
                    (new_row, new_col) not in visited):
                    new_max = max(max_elev, grid[new_row][new_col])
                    heapq.heappush(heap, (new_max, new_row, new_col))
                    visited.add((new_row, new_col))
        
        return -1
```

This solution efficiently finds the minimum time required to swim from the top-left to the bottom-right corner by always expanding the path with the smallest maximum elevation encountered so far.

This page provides a comprehensive overview of Infisical, an open-source secret management platform built to centralize application configuration and secrets (like API keys and database credentials), manage internal PKI (Public Key Infrastructure), and prevent secret leaks. This document covers the high-level architecture, core components, and how they interact within the system.

For more detailed information about specific components, please refer to other pages in this wiki: [System Architecture](#Infisical/infisical/2-system-architecture) for detailed architecture, [Secrets Management System](#Infisical/infisical/3-api-reference) for the core secrets functionality, [Workspace Management](#Infisical/infisical/4-secrets-management-system) for organization structure, and [Authentication & SSO](##5.2) for auth systems.

## Platform Purpose & Core Features

Infisical enables teams to securely manage secrets and configuration across their infrastructure with the following key capabilities:

- **Secrets Management**: Store, version, rotate, generate, and synchronize secrets
- **Internal PKI**: Create CA hierarchies and manage certificates
- **SSH**: Issue ephemeral SSH credentials
- **Identity & Access Management**: Flexible authentication and authorization controls
- **Integrations**: Connect with cloud services, CI/CD platforms, and infrastructure

The platform can be self-hosted or used as a cloud service.

Sources: [README.md40-84](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical/blob/59cffe8c/README.md#L40-L84)

## System Architecture

```
```

Infisical operates with a client-server architecture. The backend API server provides centralized services, while various clients (CLI, Web UI, Kubernetes Operator, SDKs) interact with it to access and manage secrets.

Sources: [backend/src/server/app.ts48-146](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical/blob/59cffe8c/backend/src/server/app.ts#L48-L146) [backend/src/main.ts1-110](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical/blob/59cffe8c/backend/src/main.ts#L1-L110)

## Core Components

### Backend Server

The backend is built with Node.js and TypeScript, using Fastify as the web framework. It handles request processing, authentication, and business logic for all operations.

Key components:

- **Fastify API Server**: Handles HTTP requests, routing, and middleware
- **Service Layer**: Implements business logic for core functionality
- **Data Access Layer**: Interfaces with PostgreSQL and Redis

The backend starts in `main.ts` which:

1. Loads environment configuration
2. Initializes database connections
3. Runs migrations
4. Sets up services (SMTP, Queue, KeyStore)
5. Initializes the HSM module if configured
6. Starts the Fastify server

Sources: [backend/src/main.ts21-110](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical/blob/59cffe8c/backend/src/main.ts#L21-L110) [backend/src/server/app.ts49-146](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical/blob/59cffe8c/backend/src/server/app.ts#L49-L146)

### Frontend

The frontend is a React application written in TypeScript with:

- TailwindCSS for styling
- Radix UI for accessible UI components
- React Query for data fetching
- Zustand for state management

The UI provides interfaces for managing secrets, projects, organizations, and integrations.

Sources: [frontend/package.json14-98](https://github.com/Infisical/infisical/blob/59cffe8c/frontend/package.json#L14-L98)

### Database

PostgreSQL serves as the primary database for storing:

- Encrypted secrets
- Project/workspace metadata
- Organization information
- User accounts
- Integration configurations

A separate audit log database can be configured for compliance and security monitoring.

## QuickSort Algorithm Flowchart Explanation:

**QuickSort** is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that works by:

1. **Base Case Check**: If the array has 0 or 1 elements, it's already sorted
2. **Pivot Selection**: Choose a pivot element (typically the last element)
3. **Partitioning**: Rearrange the array so elements less than the pivot come before it, and elements greater come after
4. **Recursive Sorting**: Recursively apply QuickSort to the left and right subarrays
5. **Combine**: The array is now sorted in place

### Key Features:
- **Time Complexity**: O(n log n) average case, O(n²) worst case
- **Space Complexity**: O(log n) due to recursion stack
- **In-place**: Sorts the array without requiring additional memory
- **Unstable**: Equal elements may not maintain their original order

This flowchart shows the complete algorithm flow, including the partitioning process and recursive calls that make QuickSort one of the most efficient sorting algorithms in practice.

Perfect! I've created a flowchart of the QuickSort algorithm, which is one of the fastest sorting algorithms with an average time complexity of O(n log n). Here's the flowchart:

![QuickSort Algorithm Flowchart](https://mermaid.ink/svg/eyJjb2RlIjoiZmxvd2NoYXJ0IFREXG4gICAgQVtTdGFydDogUXVpY2tTb3J0IEFsZ29yaXRobV0gLS0+IEJ7QXJyYXkgbGVuZ3RoIDw9IDE/fVxuICAgIEIgLS0-fFllc3wgQ1tSZXR1cm4gYXJyYXldXG4gICAgQiAtLT58Tm98IERbU2VsZWN0IHBpdm90IGVsZW1lbnRdXG4gICAgRCAtLT4gRVtJbml0aWFsaXplOiBpID0gbG93IC0gMV1cbiAgICBFIC0tPiBGW0ZvciBqID0gbG93IHRvIGhpZ2gtMV1cbiAgICBGIC0tPiBHe0NvbXBhcmUgZWxlbWVudCB3aXRoIHBpdm90fVxuICAgIEcgLS0-)

## QuickSort Algorithm Flowchart Explanation:

**QuickSort** is a divide-and-conquer algorithm that works by:

1. **Base Case Check**: If the array has 0 or 1 elements, it's already sorted
2. **Pivot Selection**: Choose a pivot element (typically the last element)
3. **Partitioning**: Rearrange the array so elements less than the pivot come before it, and elements greater come after
4. **Recursive Sorting**: Recursively apply QuickSort to the left and right subarrays
5. **Combine**: The array is now sorted in place

### Key Features:
- **Time Complexity**: O(n log n) average case, O(n²) worst case
- **Space Complexity**: O(log n) due to recursion stack
- **In-place**: Sorts the array without requiring additional memory
- **Unstable**: Equal elements may not maintain their original order

This flowchart shows the complete algorithm flow, including the partitioning process and recursive calls that make QuickSort one of the most efficient sorting algorithms in practice.

**Bitcoin** (abbreviation: **BTC**; [sign](/wiki/Currency_symbol "Currency symbol"): **₿**) is the first [decentralized](/wiki/Decentralized_application "Decentralized application") [cryptocurrency](/wiki/Cryptocurrency "Cryptocurrency"). Based on a [free-market](/wiki/Free-market "Free-market") ideology, bitcoin was invented in 2008 when an unknown entity published a [white paper](/wiki/White_paper "White paper") under the pseudonym of [Satoshi Nakamoto](/wiki/Satoshi_Nakamoto "Satoshi Nakamoto").[[5]](#cite_note-whoissn-7) Use of bitcoin as a [currency](/wiki/Currency "Currency") began in 2009,[[6]](#cite_note-NY2011-8) with the release of its [open-source implementation](/wiki/Open-source_software "Open-source software").[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 1 In 2021, [El Salvador adopted it as legal tender](/wiki/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador "Bitcoin in El Salvador").[[4]](#cite_note-BTCSVSept7FT-6) As bitcoin is [pseudonymous](/wiki/Pseudonym "Pseudonym"), [its use by criminals](/wiki/Cryptocurrency_and_crime "Cryptocurrency and crime") has attracted the attention of regulators, leading to [its ban by several countries](/wiki/Legality_of_cryptocurrency_by_country_or_territory "Legality of cryptocurrency by country or territory") as of 2021.[[8]](#cite_note-SunYin2019-10)

Bitcoin works through the collaboration of computers, each of which acts as a [node](/wiki/Node_(networking) "Node (networking)") in the [peer-to-peer](/wiki/Peer-to-peer "Peer-to-peer") [bitcoin network](/wiki/Bitcoin_network "Bitcoin network"). Each node maintains an independent copy of a public [distributed ledger](/wiki/Distributed_ledger "Distributed ledger") of transactions, called a [blockchain](/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain"), without central oversight. Transactions are validated through the use of [cryptography](/wiki/Cryptography "Cryptography"), preventing one person from spending another person's bitcoin, as long as the owner of the bitcoin keeps certain sensitive data secret.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 5

[Consensus](/wiki/Consensus_(computer_science) "Consensus (computer science)") between nodes about the content of the blockchain is achieved using a [computationally intensive](/wiki/Computational_complexity "Computational complexity") process based on [proof of work](/wiki/Proof_of_work "Proof of work"), called [mining](/wiki/Bitcoin_mining "Bitcoin mining"), which is performed by purpose-built computers.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 12 Mining consumes large quantities of electricity and has been criticized for [its environmental impact](/wiki/Environmental_impact_of_bitcoin "Environmental impact of bitcoin").[[9]](#cite_note-11)

## History

### Background

Before bitcoin, several [digital cash technologies](/wiki/Digital_cash "Digital cash") were released, starting with [David Chaum](/wiki/David_Chaum "David Chaum")'s [ecash](/wiki/Ecash "Ecash") in the 1980s.[[10]](#cite_note-Narayanan2017-12) The idea that solutions to computational puzzles could have some value was first proposed by cryptographers [Cynthia Dwork](/wiki/Cynthia_Dwork "Cynthia Dwork") and [Moni Naor](/wiki/Moni_Naor "Moni Naor") in 1992.[[11]](#cite_note-13)[[10]](#cite_note-Narayanan2017-12) The concept was [independently rediscovered](/wiki/Multiple_discovery "Multiple discovery") by [Adam Back](/wiki/Adam_Back "Adam Back") who developed [Hashcash](/wiki/Hashcash "Hashcash"), a [proof-of-work](/wiki/Proof-of-work "Proof-of-work") scheme for [spam control](/wiki/Anti-spam_techniques "Anti-spam techniques") in 1997.[[10]](#cite_note-Narayanan2017-12) The first proposals for distributed digital scarcity-based [cryptocurrencies](/wiki/Cryptocurrencies "Cryptocurrencies") came from [cypherpunks](/wiki/Cypherpunk "Cypherpunk") [Wei Dai](/wiki/Wei_Dai "Wei Dai") (b-money) and [Nick Szabo](/wiki/Nick_Szabo "Nick Szabo") ([bit gold](/wiki/Bit_gold "Bit gold")) in 1998.[[12]](#cite_note-14) In 2004, [Hal Finney](/wiki/Hal_Finney_(cypherpunk) "Hal Finney (cypherpunk)") developed the first currency based on reusable proof of work.[[13]](#cite_note-15) These various attempts were not successful:[[10]](#cite_note-Narayanan2017-12) Chaum's concept required centralized control and no banks wanted to sign on, Hashcash had no protection against [double-spending](/wiki/Double-spending "Double-spending"), while b-money and bit gold were not resistant to [Sybil attacks](/wiki/Sybil_attack "Sybil attack").[[10]](#cite_note-Narayanan2017-12)

### 2008–2009: Creation

### 2010–2012: Early growth

[Blockchain analysts](about:/wiki/Blockchain#Blockchain_analysis "Blockchain") estimate that Nakamoto had mined about one million bitcoins[[23]](#cite_note-25) before disappearing in 2010 when he handed the network alert key and control of the [code repository](/wiki/Software_repository "Software repository") over to [Gavin Andresen](/wiki/Gavin_Andresen "Gavin Andresen"). Andresen later became lead developer at the [Bitcoin Foundation](/wiki/Bitcoin_Foundation "Bitcoin Foundation"),[[24]](#cite_note-26)[[25]](#cite_note-27) an [organization](/wiki/List_of_bitcoin_organizations "List of bitcoin organizations") founded in September 2012 to promote bitcoin.[[26]](#cite_note-28)

After early "[proof-of-concept](/wiki/Proof-of-concept "Proof-of-concept")" transactions, the first major users of bitcoin were [black markets](/wiki/Black_market "Black market"), such as the [dark web](/wiki/Dark_web "Dark web") [Silk Road](/wiki/Silk_Road_(marketplace) "Silk Road (marketplace)"). During its 30 months of existence, beginning in February 2011, Silk Road exclusively accepted bitcoins as payment, transacting ₿9.9 million, worth about $214 million.[[27]](#cite_note-JEP-29): 222

### 2013–2014: First regulatory actions

In March 2013, the US [Financial Crimes Enforcement Network](/wiki/Financial_Crimes_Enforcement_Network "Financial Crimes Enforcement Network") (FinCEN) established regulatory guidelines for "decentralized virtual currencies" such as bitcoin, classifying American bitcoin miners who sell their generated bitcoins as [money services businesses](/wiki/Money_services_business "Money services business"), subject to registration and other legal obligations.[[28]](#cite_note-30) In May 2013, US authorities seized the unregistered [exchange](/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange "Cryptocurrency exchange") [Mt. Gox](/wiki/Mt._Gox "Mt. Gox").[[29]](#cite_note-31) In June 2013, the US [Drug Enforcement Administration](/wiki/Drug_Enforcement_Administration "Drug Enforcement Administration") seized ₿11.02 from an individual attempting to use them to purchase illicit drugs. This marked the first time a government agency had seized bitcoins.[[30]](#cite_note-32) The FBI seized about ₿30,000 in October 2013 from Silk Road, following the arrest of its founder [Ross Ulbricht](/wiki/Ross_Ulbricht "Ross Ulbricht").[[31]](#cite_note-33)

In December 2013, the [People's Bank of China](/wiki/People%27s_Bank_of_China "People's Bank of China") prohibited Chinese financial institutions from using bitcoin.[[32]](#cite_note-34) After the announcement, the value of bitcoin dropped,[[33]](#cite_note-35) and [Baidu](/wiki/Baidu "Baidu") no longer accepted bitcoins for certain services.[[34]](#cite_note-36) Buying real-world goods with any virtual currency had been illegal in China since at least 2009.[[35]](#cite_note-37)

### 2015–2019

Research produced by the [University of Cambridge](/wiki/University_of_Cambridge "University of Cambridge") estimated that in 2017, there were 2.9 to 5.8 million unique users using a [cryptocurrency wallet](/wiki/Cryptocurrency_wallet "Cryptocurrency wallet"), most of them using bitcoin.[[36]](#cite_note-38) In August 2017, the [SegWit](/wiki/SegWit "SegWit") software upgrade was activated. Segwit was intended to support the [Lightning Network](/wiki/Lightning_Network "Lightning Network") as well as improve [scalability](/wiki/Scalability "Scalability").[[37]](#cite_note-39) SegWit opponents, who supported larger blocks as a scalability solution, [forked](/wiki/Fork_(blockchain) "Fork (blockchain)") to create [Bitcoin Cash](/wiki/Bitcoin_Cash "Bitcoin Cash"), one of many [forks of bitcoin](/wiki/List_of_bitcoin_forks "List of bitcoin forks").[[38]](#cite_note-40)

In December 2017, the first [futures](/wiki/Futures_contract "Futures contract") on bitcoin was introduced by the [Chicago Mercantile Exchange](/wiki/Chicago_Mercantile_Exchange "Chicago Mercantile Exchange") (CME).[[39]](#cite_note-41)

In February 2018, the price crashed after China imposed a complete ban on bitcoin trading.[[40]](#cite_note-42) The percentage of bitcoin trading in the Chinese [renminbi](/wiki/Renminbi "Renminbi") fell from over 90% in September 2017 to less than 1% in June 2018.[[41]](#cite_note-43) During the same year, bitcoin prices were negatively affected by several hacks or thefts from cryptocurrency exchanges.[[42]](#cite_note-44)

"Square, Inc."), $50 million,[[45]](#cite_note-47) and [MassMutual](/wiki/MassMutual "MassMutual"), $100 million.[[46]](#cite_note-48) In November 2020, [PayPal](/wiki/PayPal "PayPal") added support for bitcoin in the US.[[47]](#cite_note-49)

In February 2021, bitcoin's [market capitalization](/wiki/Market_capitalization "Market capitalization") reached $1 trillion for the first time.[[48]](#cite_note-50) In November 2021, the [Taproot](/wiki/Taproot_(fork) "Taproot (fork)") [soft-fork](/wiki/Soft-fork "Soft-fork") upgrade was activated, adding support for [Schnorr signatures](/wiki/Schnorr_signature "Schnorr signature"), improved functionality of [smart contracts](/wiki/Smart_contract "Smart contract") and [Lightning Network](/wiki/Lightning_Network "Lightning Network").[[49]](#cite_note-51) Before, bitcoin only used a custom [elliptic curve](/wiki/Elliptic_curve_cryptography "Elliptic curve cryptography") with the [ECDSA](/wiki/ECDSA "ECDSA") algorithm to produce [signatures](/wiki/Digital_signature "Digital signature").[[50]](#cite_note-52): 101 In September 2021, bitcoin became [legal tender](/wiki/Legal_tender "Legal tender") in [El Salvador](/wiki/Bitcoin_in_El_Salvador "Bitcoin in El Salvador"), alongside the US dollar.[[4]](#cite_note-BTCSVSept7FT-6) In October 2021, the first bitcoin futures [exchange-traded fund](/wiki/Exchange-traded_fund "Exchange-traded fund") (ETF), called BITO, from [ProShares](/wiki/ProShares "ProShares") was approved by the [SEC](/wiki/U.S._Securities_and_Exchange_Commission "U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission") and listed on the [CME](/wiki/Chicago_Mercantile_Exchange "Chicago Mercantile Exchange").[[51]](#cite_note-53)

In early 2022, during the [Canadian trucker protests](/wiki/Canada_convoy_protest "Canada convoy protest") opposing [COVID-19 vaccine mandates](/wiki/COVID-19_vaccine_misinformation_and_hesitancy "COVID-19 vaccine misinformation and hesitancy"), organizers turned to bitcoin to receive donations after traditional financial platforms restricted access to funding.[[52]](#cite_note-54)[[53]](#cite_note-55) Proponents highlighted bitcoin's use as a tool for fundraising in situations where access to conventional financial systems may be restricted.[[54]](#cite_note-56)[[55]](#cite_note-57) In May and June 2022, the bitcoin price fell following the collapses of [TerraUSD](/wiki/Terra_(blockchain) "Terra (blockchain)"), a [stablecoin](/wiki/Stablecoin "Stablecoin"),[[56]](#cite_note-58) and the [Celsius Network](/wiki/Celsius_Network "Celsius Network"), a cryptocurrency loan company.[[57]](#cite_note-59)[[58]](#cite_note-60)

dities to be 'X'.[[67]](#cite_note-ssrn.3383734-69) XBT, a code that conforms to [ISO 4217](/wiki/ISO_4217 "ISO 4217") though not officially part of it,[[67]](#cite_note-ssrn.3383734-69) is used by [Bloomberg L.P.](/wiki/Bloomberg_L.P. "Bloomberg L.P.")[[68]](#cite_note-70)

No uniform [capitalization](/wiki/Capitalization "Capitalization") convention exists; some sources use *Bitcoin*, capitalized, to refer to the technology and [network](/wiki/Computer_network "Computer network"), and *bitcoin*, lowercase, for the unit of account.[[69]](#cite_note-71) The *[Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary](/wiki/Cambridge_Advanced_Learner%27s_Dictionary "Cambridge Advanced Learner's Dictionary")* and the *[Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary](/wiki/Oxford_Advanced_Learner%27s_Dictionary "Oxford Advanced Learner's Dictionary")* use the capitalized and lowercase variants without distinction.[[70]](#cite_note-72)[[71]](#cite_note-73)

One bitcoin is divisible to eight decimal places.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 5 Units for smaller amounts of bitcoin are the millibitcoin (mBTC), equal to 1⁄1000 bitcoin, and the satoshi[[a]](#cite_note-satoshi-2) (sat), representing 1⁄100000000 (one hundred millionth) bitcoin, the smallest amount possible.[[2]](#cite_note-satoshi_unit-3) 100,000 satoshis are one mBTC.[[72]](#cite_note-74)

### Blockchain

As a [decentralized](/wiki/Decentralization "Decentralization") system, bitcoin operates without a central authority or single administrator,[[73]](#cite_note-Gervais2014-75) so that anyone can create a new bitcoin address and transact without needing any approval.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 1 This is accomplished through a specialized [distributed ledger](/wiki/Distributed_ledger "Distributed ledger") called a *[blockchain](/wiki/Blockchain "Blockchain")* that records bitcoin transactions.[[74]](#cite_note-econbc-76)

The blockchain is implemented as an ordered list of *blocks*. Each block contains a [SHA-256](/wiki/SHA-256 "SHA-256") [hash](/wiki/Cryptographic_hash_function "Cryptographic hash function") of the previous block,[[74]](#cite_note-econbc-76) chaining them in chronological order.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 7[[74]](#cite_note-econbc-76) The blockchain is maintained by a [peer-to-peer](/wiki/Peer-to-peer "Peer-to-peer") network.[[27]](#cite_note-JEP-29): 215–219 Individual blocks, public addresses, and transactions within blocks are public information, and can be examined using a blockchain explorer.[[75]](#cite_note-77)

Nodes validate and broadcast transactions, each maintaining a copy of the blockchain for ownership verification.[[76]](#cite_note-78) A new block is created every 10 minutes on average, updating the blockchain across all nodes without central oversight. This process tracks bitcoin spending, ensuring each bitcoin is [spent only once](/wiki/Double-spending "Double-spending"). Unlike a traditional ledger that tracks physical currency, bitcoins exist digitally as [unspent outputs of transactions](/wiki/Unspent_outputs_of_transactions "Unspent outputs of transactions").[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 5

### Addresses and transactions

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/c/ce/Bitcoin_Transaction_Visual.svg/250px-Bitcoin_Transaction_Visual.svg.png)](/wiki/File:Bitcoin_Transaction_Visual.svg)

Simplified chain of ownership. In practice, a transaction can have more than one input and more than one output.[[77]](#cite_note-EconOfBTC-79)

In the blockchain, bitcoins are linked to specific [strings](/wiki/String_(computer_science) "String (computer science)") called addresses. Most often, an address encodes a [hash](/wiki/Hash_(cryptography) "Hash (cryptography)") of a single [public key](/wiki/Public_key "Public key"). Creating such an address involves generating a random private key and then computing the corresponding address. This process is almost instant, but the reverse (finding the private key for a given address) is nearly impossible.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 4 Publishing such a bitcoin address does not risk its private key, and it is extremely unlikely to accidentally generate a used key with funds. To use bitcoins, owners need their private key to [digitally sign](/wiki/Digital_signature "Digital signature") transactions, which are verified by the network using the public key, keeping the private key secret.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 5 An address may encode the hash of a bitcoin script that specifies more complex requirements to spend the funds. One common example is "multisig", in which multiple distinct private keys must mutually sign any transaction that attempts to spend the funds.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 7

Bitcoin transactions use a [Forth](/wiki/Forth_(programming_language) "Forth (programming language)")-like [scripting language](/wiki/Scripting_language "Scripting language"),[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 5 involving one or more inputs and outputs. When sending bitcoins, a user specifies the recipients' addresses and the amount for each output. This allows sending bitcoins to several recipients in a single transaction. To prevent double-spending, each input must refer to a previous unspent output in the blockchain.[[77]](#cite_note-EconOfBTC-79) Using multiple inputs is similar to using multiple coins in a cash transaction. As in a cash transaction, the sum of inputs can exceed the intended sum of payments. In such a case, an additional output can return the change back to the payer.[[77]](#cite_note-EconOfBTC-79) Unallocated input satoshis in the transaction become the transaction fee.[[77]](#cite_note-EconOfBTC-79)

Losing a private key means losing access to the bitcoins, with no other proof of ownership accepted by the [protocol](/wiki/Bitcoin_protocol "Bitcoin protocol").[[27]](#cite_note-JEP-29) For instance, in 2013, a user lost ₿7,500, valued at US$7.5 million, by accidentally discarding a [hard drive](/wiki/Hard_disk_drive "Hard disk drive") with the private key.[[78]](#cite_note-80) It is estimated that around 20% of all bitcoins are lost.[[79]](#cite_note-81) The private key must also be kept secret as its exposure, such as through a [data breach](/wiki/Data_breach "Data breach"), can lead to theft of the associated bitcoins.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 10[[80]](#cite_note-82) As of December 2017, approximately ₿980,000 had been stolen from [cryptocurrency exchanges](/wiki/Cryptocurrency_exchange "Cryptocurrency exchange").[[81]](#cite_note-83)

### Mining

[![](//upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/b/b3/Argo_Blockchain_Mirabel_Facility.jpg/250px-Argo_Blockchain_Mirabel_Facility.jpg)](/wiki/File:Argo_Blockchain_Mirabel_Facility.jpg)

Bitcoin mining [facility](/wiki/Data_center "Data center") with large amounts of mining hardware

Miners don't directly act as nodes, but do communicate with nodes. The mining process is primarily intended to prevent [double-spending](/wiki/Double-spending "Double-spending") and get all nodes to agree on the content of the blockchain, but it also has desirable side-effects such as making it infeasible for adversaries to stifle valid transactions or alter the historical record of transactions, since doing so generally requires the adversary to have access to more mining power than the rest of the network combined.[[7]](#cite_note-Antonopoulos2014-9): ch. 12

The mining process in bitcoin involves maintaining the blockchain through computer [processing power](/wiki/Processing_power "Processing power"). Miners group and broadcast new transactions into blocks, which are then verified by the network.[[74]](#cite_note-econbc-76) Each block must contain a proof of work (PoW) to be accepted,[[74]](#cite_note-econbc-76) involving finding a [nonce](/wiki/Cryptographic_nonce "Cryptographic nonce") number that, combined with the block content, produces a [hash](/w...(内容已截断)

[Bitcoin](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/article/an-intro-to-bitcoin) is a decentralized [cryptocurrency](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/article/what-are-cryptocurrencies) originally described in a 2008 [whitepaper](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/glossary/whitepaper) by a person, or group of people, using the alias [Satoshi Nakamoto](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/article/who-is-satoshi-nakamoto). It was launched soon after, in January 2009.

[Bitcoin](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/article/what-is-bitcoin) is a peer-to-peer online currency, meaning that all [transactions](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/article/how-long-does-a-bitcoin-transaction-take) happen directly between equal, independent network participants, without the need for any intermediary to permit or facilitate them. Bitcoin was created, according to Nakamoto’s own words, to allow “online payments to be sent directly from one party to another without going through a financial institution.”

Some concepts for a similar type of a decentralized electronic currency precede BTC, but Bitcoin holds the distinction of being the [first-ever cryptocurrency](https://coinmarketcap.com/alexandria/article/a-beginner-s-guide-to-investing-in-cryptocurrencies) to come into actual use.
